newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian crude shrugs off Deng, falls on stock news.
newsitem.headline: Asian crude shrugs off Deng, falls on stock news.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia were lower on Thursday, unperturbed by the death of Deng Xiaoping and focusing instead on bearish stock data from the United States, traders said.
China announced the death of its paramount leader late on Wednesday, marking the end of an 18-year rule that transformed China from a backward Stalinist state to an economic powerhourse.

"Headlines are around, but there has been no reaction in oil and I would not expect one," a broker on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), which trades the benchmark Brent crude oil futures contract, said.
"I don't see any effect on the market," a Japanese trader said.
The key April Brent contract on SIMEX was untraded at 0530 GMT but was quoted at $20.46/$20.56 per barrel, down from London's overnight close of $20.63.
Traders said the decline followed stock data released late in New York on Wednesday from the American Petroleum Institute (API).
The data -- released after the end of New York trading -- showed a rise in crude oil stocks of 3.12 million barrels, surpassing some expectations and indication more available supplies.
New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) crude futures, trading on the after-hours trading system ACCESS, fell after the stock data were released.
The most active March NYMEX contract was last traded at 0530 GMT at $22.57 per barrel, down 22 cents from New York's closing level.
Oil products markets in Asia also shrugged off the news of Deng's death, but it proved a major talking point for brokers as they tried to drum up business in Singapore.

"Those who were long said the death will lead to an increase of gas oil during the funeral and those who were short said demand would drop as factories close down," one broker said. China's has announced six days of mourning to mark Deng's death.
Traders said they did not expect any change in China's crude oil and products trading patterns. The country is a net import of both.
In a wider context, analysts and industry sources said they expected little impact on the energy sector from Deng's death.
They said Deng had been a figurehead for some years and his age and reports of failing health had led financial sectors to factor in his loss.
In addition, the process of foreign investment into China's energy sector is a long slow process that was unlikely to be troubled by Deng's death.
